title: A justice once blocked a polling place; forty years later it was a national tactic
dek: Rehnquist challenged Black voters' eligibility in Phoenix in 1962, and two years later the playbook became a nationwide "Operation Eagle Eye"; meanwhile Arab workers in Detroit turned a wildcat strike into political power grown from the factory floor.
why: Two storylines lay out the two paths of the American voting-rights fight: top-down suppression and bottom-up organizing. Medium information density; the Michigan story in the back half is the more valuable one.
who: Readers interested in the American electoral system, the voting-rights fight and grassroots political organizing; people working on political risk, community mobilization or labor research.
skip: The NPR program-promotion segments at the start and in the middle can be skipped.

points.h: The future chief justice stopped people at the polls
points.body: At Rehnquist's 1986 confirmation hearings, the most dramatic part was not his 14 years on the bench but what he did in Phoenix in the 1960s. Witnesses said he stood outside a polling place, walked up to a Black voter and asked "Are you a qualified voter," demanding the person show identification and read aloud a passage of the Constitution. Rehnquist denied at the hearings that he had harassed or intimidated voters, but acknowledged he had given legal advice to Republicans challenging voters' eligibility at polling places, and sometimes showed up in person. He called it an "election day project"; others called it a "ballot security program." That project later became a national strategy.

points.h: His conservatism took shape in high school
points.body: Journalist John A. Jenkins was doing interviews for a Rehnquist biography when his editor told him to dig into "the origins of his conservatism." Rehnquist was born in 1924 in Shorewood, Wisconsin, an all-white community, and went to an all-white high school. He was a high school senior at the time of Pearl Harbor; he organized a school assembly called "Wake Up America," joined patriotic groups, and signed up as a block captain to report subversive activity to the FBI. After the war he entered Stanford Law School, finished first in his class, and then clerked for Supreme Court Justice Robert Jackson. Five months later, in 1952, the 28-year-old wrote a memo telling Jackson: in Brown v. Board you need not vote with the majority; there is a more principled position.

points.h: He saw integration as a personal choice, not a federal matter
points.body: Rehnquist's position was that integration was a matter of personal choice, not something to be imposed on people, and that it should be decided by the states, not the federal government. This was a classic conservative stance, and it helped establish him among Republican rising stars as an ideological purist. He carried that philosophy with him to Phoenix, which was still grappling with Jim Crow laws and an emerging civil rights movement. When the city council passed an anti-discrimination ordinance, he wrote letters to the editor and spoke at meetings, was noticed, and was encouraged to enter politics. That meant extra scrutiny of voters in Democratic-leaning precincts — Republicans believed many of them were voting illegally.

points.h: The voter-challenge playbook: returned mail, then challengers at the polls
points.body: Tova Wang, research project director at Harvard Kennedy School's Ash Center, read FBI background-check excerpts: two white Republican challengers, one of them allegedly Rehnquist, at a polling place in an elementary school named for civil rights leader Mary McLeod Bethune on November 6, 1962, facing Black and minority voters, holding up a card with a passage from the Constitution and demanding they read it to prove literacy. The method was: first mail letters into Democratic precincts, and if the mail came back, send challengers to the polls to question eligibility. According to one FBI interview, the plan was to send large numbers of challengers into minority Democratic precincts at peak hours to clog the polling places, intimidate voters, or stall them until they gave up. Arizona law allowed each party to send representatives to challenge suspect voters, but eligibility was ultimately decided by election officials.

points.h: Operation Eagle Eye: 1.25 million voters challenged nationwide
points.body: In the 1964 election, Republicans rolled out "Operation Eagle Eye." Its director, Charles Barr, told media including The New York Times that he expected to challenge or deter 1.25 million voters nationwide. The blueprint was the same as Phoenix: mail into Democratic precincts, and if it came back, challenge at the polls. On election day, The New York Times reported Republican officials saying 100,000 trained Republican workers were deployed across 35 key cities. The Miami Herald wrote that "hundreds upon hundreds of voters were confused and frightened into partisan poll-watching." The New York Times said the operation was launched in nearly every state. The FBI was asked to investigate leaflets distributed in Black precincts, aimed at creating delay, confusion and fear.

points.h: Goldwater lost; Rehnquist was playing a long game
points.body: Rehnquist persuaded Goldwater to oppose and vote against the Civil Rights Act, which became a symbol of Goldwater's extreme conservatism, and even some in his own party began to abandon him. But Rehnquist did not. Goldwater was routed, and Rehnquist wrote his concession speech. The judgment in the episode is: Rehnquist did not care how others saw him, would rather be defeated on an issue than compromise, and believed he could win it back later — he was playing a long game. In 1971, at 47, he was nominated to the Supreme Court, and at his confirmation hearings the voter-suppression allegations did not hold up for lack of evidence. At his 1986 confirmation as chief justice, new witnesses appeared, including former federal assistant prosecutor James Brosnahan, but it remained one side's word against the other. He served on the Supreme Court for 33 years, until his death in 2005.

points.h: Beside the Ford plant, a neighborhood held off bulldozers with a human chain
points.body: Ismael Ahmed's father came from Egypt to New York at age 10 on a freighter, and no one asked him any questions when he disembarked. In the 1950s the family moved to Detroit, settling in Dearborn's South End — a narrow strip wedged between the Ford Rouge plant and the city of Detroit. At its peak the Rouge plant had 90,000 workers. In the 1960s, the Edward C. Levy company used Ford waste to make asphalt, and big trucks drove through the neighborhood, spilling waste off open truck beds. After residents protested, the city decided to rezone the neighborhood as heavy industrial, which satisfied Ford and Levy and drove out the complainers. Arab residents began to fight back: when bulldozers came to tear down houses, women and children formed a human chain across the street. They held the line block by block, house by house.

points.h: Wildcat strike: the union bought Israel bonds, the workers walked
points.body: The Arab Workers Caucus discovered that their local UAW had bought more than $300,000 in Israel bonds, and the national union had bought far more. That meant roughly 15,000 Arab members of the UAW were paying to support what they saw as a violent occupation. They ran an ad in the Detroit Free Press: these workers saw the purchase of Israel bonds the way Black workers saw the UAW investing in apartheid South Africa. They petitioned the UAW with no result, then learned that UAW president Leonard Woodcock was to receive an award at a ceremony, and decided to organize a wildcat strike — a strike without the union's permission. After more than a month of organizing, on November 28, 1973, about 2,000 workers walked out of the Dodge main plant, not only Arabs but also Black workers. That evening about 1,000 Arabs picketed outside the awards ceremony, and Woodcock slipped in through a back door. The UAW later sold off some of the bonds, though not all of them.

terms.def: The Republicans' nationwide polling-place challenge program in the 1964 election, aiming to challenge or deter 1.25 million voters.
A strike launched by rank-and-file members on their own, without the permission of union leadership.
An organization of Arab workers in Detroit auto plants that launched the 1973 wildcat strike.
The main union in the American auto industry, protested by its Arab members in 1973 over its purchase of Israel bonds.
